neutral_facts.value: The accused, a man, was married to a woman who died along with her child by drowning in a river within seven years of their marriage. The prosecution alleged that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty and harassment related to dowry demands. The deceased visited her sister's house and called her father, reporting harassment. The father and sister testified about the harassment, and a doctor opined that the death occurred around February 16-17, 2001. The trial court convicted the accused under s.304-B IPC, but the High Court reduced the sentence. The accused claimed there was no cruelty or dowry demand, but the courts found the evidence of harassment sufficient to invoke the presumption under s.113-B of the Evidence Act.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in an appeal under Article 136, the Court will not reassess the evidence at large, particularly when it has been concurrently accepted by the High Court and the Courts below, and that the Court will not interfere unless there is a violation of principles of natural justice, error of law or procedure, misreading of evidence, or the conclusion of the High Court is manifestly perverse and unsupportable.

quotes.text: In various Supreme Court judgments, it has been held that in an appeal u/Art.136, the Court will not reassess the evidence at large, particularly, when it has been concurrently accepted by the High Court and the Courts below.

sentencing_rationale.value: The final sentence was imposed based on the trial court's and high court's findings that the accused had committed dowry death under Section 304-B of the IPC, and that the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act was not rebutted.

quotes.text: The law enjoins under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act drawing of the presumption that the accused has committed the dowry death. The view taken by trial Court and affirmed by the High Court on basis of the material available on record cannot be said to be manifestly perverse.
